characteristics.roast: Dry pan-firing in a cast-iron wok (not considered roasting in the oolong sense)
characteristics.harvestSeason: Early spring (the finest harvest is pre-Qingming, early April)

description.short: Flat green tea with a chestnut aroma and a mellow, sweet flavor
description.overview: One of China's Ten Famous Teas. Its uniqueness comes from hand pan-firing in a hot cast-iron wok, which imparts the distinctive flattened sword-like shape to the leaves.
description.leaf: Flat, smooth, light-green leaves resembling the shape of a sword blade
description.liquor: Light yellow-green, clear, and bright liquor
description.aroma: Toasted chestnut, fresh spring grass, delicate sweetness
description.taste: Mellow, delicately sweet, with nutty and roasted chestnut notes, free of bitterness when brewed at proper temperature
description.aftertaste: Fresh, subtly sweet, clean and refreshing
description.processing: Plucking of one bud with 1–2 leaves → brief withering → hand-firing and shaping in a hot wok (shaqing and flattening simultaneously) → final drying

history.origin: The name means 'Dragon Well' — named after a well in a village near West Lake where, according to legend, a benevolent dragon resided
history.development: Documented as early as the Tang dynasty, Longjing gained widespread renown during the Qing dynasty
history.modern: During the 18th century, Emperor Qianlong visited a temple near West Lake, praised tea picked from 18 bushes, and granted them imperial status; these bushes are preserved today as protected heritage trees
interestingFacts: Authentic Longjing from the West Lake protected origin carries a protected geographical indication and is far more expensive than teas processed with the same method in other regions
Skilled tea masters shape the leaves with bare hands inside a wok heated to around 200°C, a craft requiring years of dedicated training
